title: Upper GI Bleeding: Perfusion Before the Stool Color
bottomLine: GI bleeding becomes an emergency when perfusion is failing. Assess hemodynamics, mental status, ongoing hematemesis/melena, anticoagulant use and hemoglobin trend; establish ordered access/fluids/blood pathway and prepare for endoscopic control. A normal first hemoglobin does not exclude major acute blood loss.
recognize: Hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena; brisk upper bleeding can present with hematochezia
Tachycardia, orthostasis, hypotension, pallor, diaphoresis, syncope
NSAIDs, anticoagulants, liver disease/varices, prior ulcer increase risk
assess: ABCs, BP/HR/perfusion, mental status, SpO2, amount/frequency of bleeding
Review anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs and last doses
Trend CBC, coagulation, BUN/creatinine and crossmatch as ordered
actions: Keep unstable patient NPO and activate GI/emergency pathway
Obtain large-bore IV access when ordered/within role and give prescribed fluids/blood
Administer ordered IV PPI; variceal pathway may include vasoactive therapy and antibiotics
Prepare for urgent endoscopy
diagnostics: Endoscopy both diagnoses and treats many upper GI sources
Hemoglobin may initially appear near baseline before equilibration; clinical perfusion and trend matter
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant reversal is indication/drug specific
NSAIDs increase ulcer/bleeding risk
Octreotide/vasoactive therapy is used for suspected variceal bleeding under protocol
teaching: Avoid nonprescribed NSAID overuse, follow ulcer/H. pylori treatment, and take antithrombotics only as directed
Return urgently for recurrent hematemesis, black stool with weakness, syncope or dyspnea
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN priorities are perfusion assessment, ordered resuscitation/medication administration, accurate bleeding output and escalation. Endoscopic/reversal strategy is team-directed.
examTrap: Waiting for the hemoglobin to fall before treating a pale hypotensive patient with active hematemesis.
oneLinePearl: GI bleed: treat perfusion and ongoing loss, not one lab value.
sourceBasis: American College of Gastroenterology upper GI bleeding guideline

title: Cirrhosis: Portal Pressure, Fluid, Bleeding, Infection, Brain
bottomLine: Decompensated cirrhosis is not just jaundice: watch ascites/edema, variceal bleeding, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, kidney dysfunction and malnutrition. New GI bleeding, fever/abdominal pain, confusion, hypotension or declining urine output needs urgent escalation.
recognize: Ascites, edema, jaundice, spider angiomas, bruising, sarcopenia
Portal hypertension: splenomegaly, varices, thrombocytopenia
Encephalopathy: sleep reversal, confusion, asterixis
SBP may present with fever, abdominal pain/tenderness, encephalopathy or renal decline
assess: Daily weight/abdominal girth when ordered, edema, lung sounds, intake/output
Mental status/asterixis, stool/bleeding, infection signs
Trend sodium, creatinine, bilirubin, INR, albumin, CBC as ordered
actions: Follow sodium/fluid/diuretic plan and monitor renal/electrolyte response
For suspected variceal bleed: emergency GI pathway
For new ascites deterioration/fever: prepare for diagnostic paracentesis
Administer lactulose/rifaximin and antibiotics as ordered
diagnostics: Paracentesis evaluates new/worsening ascites for infection
Endoscopy screens/treats varices
Ammonia level alone does not define encephalopathy severity; clinical mental status matters
medicationSafety: Diuretics can cause AKI/electrolyte disturbance
Nonselective beta blockers reduce variceal risk in selected patients but require BP/HR monitoring
Avoid unnecessary sedatives/NSAIDs and review hepatotoxic drugs
teaching: No alcohol, medication/OTC review, nutrition plan, daily weights if instructed, and urgent reporting of bleeding/confusion/fever
Do not intentionally restrict protein for routine encephalopathy without the current nutrition plan
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors decompensation, administers ordered therapy and reinforces the cirrhosis plan. Paracentesis/endoscopy/transplant decisions are specialist-directed.
examTrap: Treating an ammonia number instead of assessing new confusion for bleeding, infection, constipation, dehydration, drugs and other triggers.
oneLinePearl: Cirrhosis complications: bleed, belly infection/fluid, brain, kidney.

title: Hepatic Encephalopathy: Find the Trigger, Clear the Nitrogen Load Safely
bottomLine: Hepatic encephalopathy is a clinical syndrome of altered cognition in severe liver dysfunction. Treat the precipitant—GI bleed, infection, constipation, dehydration, kidney failure, sedatives, electrolyte disturbance—and give ordered lactulose/rifaximin while protecting airway, falls and aspiration. Do not chase ammonia values in isolation.
recognize: Sleep reversal, slowed thinking, personality change, disorientation, asterixis, somnolence
Triggers often matter more than the baseline cirrhosis severity
Severe encephalopathy can impair airway protection
assess: Mental status trend, asterixis, airway/swallow safety, fall risk
Bowel pattern and lactulose response
Look for bleeding, fever/infection, volume depletion, renal/electrolyte problems, sedating meds
actions: Protect airway/aspiration and safety
Give lactulose to the ordered stool target and rifaximin when prescribed
Treat the trigger and avoid unnecessary sedatives
Escalate progressive somnolence or inability to protect airway
diagnostics: Ammonia can be elevated without encephalopathy and may not correlate with severity
Labs/cultures/imaging target precipitating causes
medicationSafety: Excess lactulose can cause diarrhea, dehydration and electrolyte loss, which can worsen encephalopathy
Benzodiazepines/opioids can worsen mental status/ventilation
teaching: Take lactulose/rifaximin as prescribed, track bowel pattern, avoid unapproved sedatives/alcohol, and seek care for new confusion
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors cognition/bowel response and precipitating bedside causes, administers ordered therapy and escalates. Medication titration beyond explicit parameters requires clarification.
examTrap: Increasing lactulose endlessly because ammonia remains high despite profuse diarrhea and worsening dehydration.
oneLinePearl: Encephalopathy: treat the trigger and the patient, not the ammonia number.

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Pain Plus Systemic Inflammation
bottomLine: Acute pancreatitis ranges from self-limited inflammation to shock, respiratory failure, kidney injury and necrosis. Give goal-directed fluids as ordered, control pain/nausea, monitor organ function and begin enteral/oral nutrition as tolerated rather than prolonged routine NPO when severe ileus/procedure does not require it.
recognize: Severe persistent epigastric pain often radiating to back, nausea/vomiting
Common causes include gallstones and alcohol; also hypertriglyceridemia, medications and procedures
Severe disease: hypotension, hypoxemia, oliguria, SIRS, organ failure
assess: Pain, vitals/perfusion, oxygenation, urine output, hydration
Glucose, calcium, renal function, hematocrit and other severity labs as ordered
Assess respiratory deterioration/abdominal distention and infection signs
actions: Administer ordered IV fluids while reassessing overload/perfusion
Provide multimodal analgesia/antiemetics
Early oral/enteral nutrition when tolerated per plan
Treat gallstone obstruction or other cause through specialist pathway
diagnostics: Diagnosis usually requires typical pain plus elevated lipase/amylase and/or characteristic imaging
Routine repeat lipase does not track clinical recovery
CT is not mandatory for every uncomplicated early case
medicationSafety: Opioids require respiratory/sedation monitoring
Prophylactic antibiotics are not routine for sterile necrotizing pancreatitis
Monitor glucose with pancreatic stress
teaching: Avoid alcohol if implicated, follow gallstone/lipid treatment, stop smoking, and seek care for recurrent severe pain/vomiting
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN provides symptom/supportive care, fluid/urine monitoring, ordered nutrition and escalation. Decisions about ERCP/drainage/surgery are team-directed.
examTrap: Keeping every pancreatitis patient NPO for days solely because the pancreas needs to 'rest,' despite improving symptoms and an order to resume enteral nutrition.
oneLinePearl: Pancreatitis severity is organ failure—not the lipase height.
sourceBasis: American College of Gastroenterology Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

title: Gallbladder vs Cholangitis: Fever and Jaundice Raise the Stakes
bottomLine: RUQ pain after meals with fever/tenderness can be acute cholecystitis; jaundice with fever/systemic illness suggests common-duct obstruction/cholangitis and can become septic. Keep acutely ill patients NPO as ordered, give fluids/analgesia/antibiotics, and escalate obstructive sepsis for urgent biliary drainage.
recognize: Cholecystitis: RUQ pain, fever, nausea/vomiting, Murphy-type tenderness
Cholangitis: fever, jaundice, RUQ pain; hypotension/confusion indicate severe disease
Gallstone pancreatitis can coexist
assess: Vitals/perfusion, pain, jaundice, abdominal findings, hydration
Trend bilirubin/liver enzymes, CBC, lipase, renal function
Assess sepsis/mental status
actions: NPO initially when ordered, IV fluids/analgesia/antiemetics
Administer antibiotics for infection
Prepare for cholecystectomy or urgent ERCP/biliary drainage depending on diagnosis
diagnostics: Ultrasound is first-line for gallbladder disease
MRCP/EUS/ERCP address common-duct questions; ERCP is therapeutic but invasive
medicationSafety: Opioid/antiemetic sedation monitoring
Antibiotic allergies/renal function
Do not use antibiotics as a substitute for source control in obstructive cholangitis
teaching: Post-treatment diet/activity instructions, warning signs of recurrent jaundice/fever, and follow-up for gallstones
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN recognizes sepsis/obstruction, administers ordered therapy and prepares for procedures. ERCP/surgical decisions are specialist-directed.
examTrap: Treating fever and jaundice as routine biliary colic and waiting for the pain to pass.
oneLinePearl: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice = think infected obstruction.

title: Bowel Obstruction: Distention, Vomiting, and the Strangulation Red Flags
bottomLine: Mechanical bowel obstruction causes pain, distention, vomiting and reduced stool/flatus, but the emergency is strangulation/ischemia/perforation. NPO, decompress with ordered NG tube when indicated, replace fluids/electrolytes, monitor output and escalate continuous severe pain, fever, peritonitis, lactate rise, tachycardia or shock.
recognize: Crampy pain, distention, vomiting, constipation/obstipation
Early high-pitched/tinkling bowel sounds are not required and later obstruction may be quiet
Strangulation clues: continuous pain, tenderness/peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis/acidosis, shock
assess: Vitals/perfusion, abdominal distention/pain/tenderness, vomiting, stool/flatus
NG output and tube function if present
Strict intake/output, electrolytes, renal function, hydration
actions: Keep NPO and give prescribed IV fluids/electrolytes
NG decompression as ordered
Antiemetic/analgesia without masking ongoing reassessment
Prepare for urgent surgery when ischemia/perforation/closed-loop obstruction suspected
diagnostics: CT often defines site/cause/complications
Labs assess dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, ischemia/infection
medicationSafety: Avoid laxatives/enemas in suspected complete obstruction/perforation unless specifically directed
Opioids can worsen ileus and obscure changes; use ordered analgesia with reassessment
redFlags: Sudden pain relief followed by deterioration suggesting perforation
teaching: After resolution/surgery, follow diet/activity plan and report recurrent vomiting/distention/no flatus
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors abdomen/NG/output/fluids, gives ordered therapy and escalates strangulation signs. Do not independently advance diet or clamp/remove NG tube outside the plan.
examTrap: Giving a stimulant laxative for constipation when the patient has severe distention, vomiting and suspected complete obstruction.
oneLinePearl: Obstruction is uncomfortable; strangulation is deadly—watch pain pattern, tenderness and perfusion.
sourceBasis: American College of Surgeons/emergency surgery obstruction guidance

title: Appendicitis and Peritonitis: A Changing Pain Pattern Matters
bottomLine: Appendicitis often progresses from vague periumbilical discomfort to localized RLQ pain, but presentations vary. Sudden pain relief followed by diffuse pain, rigidity, fever or toxicity can signal perforation/peritonitis. Keep suspected surgical abdomen NPO and avoid heating pads, laxatives or enemas while urgent evaluation occurs.
recognize: Migrating/localized abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, low fever
Older adults/pregnancy can present atypically
Peritonitis: guarding/rigidity, rebound, severe diffuse tenderness, ileus, fever, tachycardia
assess: Vitals/perfusion, pain onset/migration, abdominal findings, nausea/vomiting/stool
Pregnancy possibility and urinary/gynecologic differential
Watch for sepsis and abrupt change in pain
actions: NPO, IV fluids/analgesia/antiemetic and antibiotics as ordered
Prepare for surgical evaluation
Escalate perforation/sepsis signs immediately
diagnostics: CT or ultrasound depending on age/pregnancy/context
CBC/CRP/urinalysis/pregnancy testing support differential but no single lab proves appendicitis
medicationSafety: Appropriate analgesia does not need to be withheld solely to preserve the exam
Avoid nonordered laxatives/enemas when acute surgical abdomen suspected
teaching: Postoperative wound/activity instructions and return precautions for fever, worsening pain, vomiting or wound infection
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs serial focused abdominal assessment and pre/post-op care, administers orders and escalates changes. Surgical diagnosis/decision is provider-directed.
examTrap: Applying a heating pad or giving a laxative because the patient has RLQ pain and constipation.
oneLinePearl: Surgical abdomen: NPO, no heat/laxatives, watch for perforation.

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Flare, Bleeding, Nutrition, and Toxic Megacolon
bottomLine: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis cause inflammatory flares with diarrhea, abdominal pain, bleeding, weight loss and extraintestinal disease. The dangerous change is systemic toxicity, severe distention/tenderness, major bleeding, dehydration or perforation—possible severe colitis/toxic megacolon requiring urgent escalation.
recognize: UC: continuous colonic mucosal disease with bloody diarrhea
Crohn: any GI segment, skip/transmural disease with strictures/fistulas
Both can cause anemia, malnutrition, arthritis, skin/eye/hepatobiliary manifestations
assess: Stool frequency/blood, abdominal pain/distention, fever, weight/hydration
CBC, electrolytes, inflammatory markers and nutrition labs as ordered
Medication infection risk and steroid effects
actions: Hydration/electrolyte/nutrition support
Administer anti-inflammatory/immunomodulator/biologic therapy as ordered
Avoid unnecessary antidiarrheals in severe colitis/toxic megacolon concern
Escalate obstruction, perforation, severe bleeding or toxic megacolon
diagnostics: Stool tests exclude infection including C. difficile during flares
Endoscopy/imaging define extent/complications
medicationSafety: Biologics/immunosuppressants require infection screening/monitoring
Steroids are for induction/flare treatment rather than ideal long-term maintenance
NSAIDs may worsen symptoms in some patients
teaching: Medication adherence, vaccination/infection precautions for immunosuppression, nutrition plan, smoking cessation especially in Crohn disease, cancer-surveillance follow-up
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN tracks stool/bleeding/hydration and medication effects, provides ordered support, and reports severe-colitis complications. Immunotherapy selection is GI-specialist directed.
examTrap: Giving an antidiarrheal automatically to a patient with severe distention, fever and suspected toxic megacolon.
oneLinePearl: IBD flare is inflammation; distention + toxicity is an emergency.
sourceBasis: American College of Gastroenterology ulcerative colitis/Crohn disease guidelines

title: Ostomy Care: Stoma Perfusion, Output, and Skin
bottomLine: A healthy new stoma is moist and pink/red; dusky, purple, black, very pale or rapidly worsening appearance can mean perfusion compromise. Protect peristomal skin, fit the barrier close to the stoma, measure output, and recognize high-output dehydration risk especially with ileostomy.
recognize: New stoma edema is expected initially; color/perfusion is the key
Ileostomy output is liquid/enzymatic and can cause fluid/electrolyte loss
Colostomy output varies with segment
Skin should not be chronically exposed to effluent
assess: Stoma color/moisture/swelling, output amount/character, peristomal skin
Hydration, urine output, weight and electrolytes with high output
Post-op abdominal pain/distention and return of bowel function
actions: Empty pouch before overly full and size barrier appropriately
Use skin-protection products as indicated
Escalate ischemic stoma or absent output with obstructive symptoms
Replace fluids/electrolytes according to plan for high-output ileostomy
diagnostics: Labs evaluate dehydration/electrolyte loss when output is high; imaging evaluates obstruction when clinically indicated
medicationSafety: Extended-release/enteric medications may have absorption issues in some ileostomy patients; report intact tablets and consult pharmacy
Antidiarrheal/high-output medications are individualized and ordered
teaching: Pouching technique, hydration signs, diet progression, odor/gas management, body-image support and ostomy nurse resources
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs routine ostomy care, measures output and identifies stoma/skin complications. Complex fitting and new severe complications may need wound/ostomy specialist/surgical review.
examTrap: Calling a dusky postoperative stoma normal because swelling is expected.
oneLinePearl: Stoma: pink/red and moist; protect skin and watch output.

title: C. difficile: Diarrhea Plus Antibiotic Exposure Needs Contact Control
bottomLine: New clinically significant diarrhea after antibiotics or healthcare exposure can be C. difficile. Use appropriate Contact Precautions, soap-and-water handwashing when caring for suspected/confirmed C. difficile especially after contamination/outbreak per facility/CDC guidance, obtain the correct unformed stool specimen, stop unnecessary inciting antibiotics through the care team, and monitor dehydration/toxic colitis.
recognize: Watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, fever/leukocytosis after antibiotic exposure
Severe disease may cause ileus, distention, toxic megacolon, shock
Do not test formed stool or asymptomatic colonization routinely
assess: Stool frequency/character, abdominal distention/tenderness, fever, hydration/urine output
Recent antibiotics, PPIs, hospitalization/long-term care
CBC/creatinine and severity markers as ordered
actions: Contact Precautions and dedicated equipment according to facility policy
Environmental sporicidal cleaning per infection-control plan
Administer oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin or other ordered therapy
Escalate ileus/toxic megacolon/shock
diagnostics: Test only appropriate symptomatic unformed stool using the facility algorithm
Repeat testing for cure is not routine when symptoms resolve
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and antiperistaltic agents in severe colitis/ileus unless specifically directed
Recurrent infection management differs from first episode
teaching: Handwashing, bathroom/environmental hygiene, complete treatment, and do not self-treat recurrent diarrhea with leftover antibiotics
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN initiates/maintains precautions per policy, measures stools/fluids, administers ordered treatment and reports severe-colitis signs. Testing/treatment selection follows the clinical pathway.
examTrap: Sending a formed stool specimen for C. difficile testing in a patient without clinically significant diarrhea.
oneLinePearl: C. diff: isolate the diarrhea, test the right stool, watch for toxic colon.

title: Enteral Feeding: Aspiration Prevention and Tube Safety
bottomLine: Enteral feeding is preferred when the gut works, but aspiration, tube misplacement, clogging and refeeding/electrolyte problems can cause harm. Verify tube placement using the approved method before use, keep the patient appropriately elevated when not contraindicated, flush as ordered, and never use air-bolus auscultation as proof of gastric placement.
recognize: Aspiration risk rises with impaired consciousness/swallow, vomiting, supine position, reflux and some gastric-motility problems
New cough, dyspnea, desaturation, fever or formula-like secretions can signal aspiration
Severely malnourished patients can develop refeeding electrolyte shifts
assess: Tube position/marking and placement verification per tube type/policy
Abdominal tolerance, nausea/vomiting/distention, stool, hydration
Respiratory status and head-of-bed position
Phosphate, potassium, magnesium/glucose in high refeeding-risk patients as ordered
actions: Elevate head during feeding and for the prescribed period afterward when safe
Flush tube with water per order/policy before/between/after medications
Stop feeding and assess/escalate suspected aspiration or tube displacement
Use pump/rate prescribed and avoid unapproved rapid boluses
diagnostics: Initial NG/feeding tube placement often requires radiographic confirmation before first use depending on tube/location and policy
Bedside pH/other approved methods may support ongoing position checks; auscultating injected air is unreliable
medicationSafety: Do not crush enteric-coated, extended-release, hazardous or otherwise non-crushable medications
Give medications separately rather than mixing all together with formula
Check feed-drug interactions and whether feeding must be paused
teaching: Home tube users need placement/flush/skin care and aspiration warning signs according to the device plan
scopeAndDelegation: Tube feeding/medication administration requires competency and policy. PN/LVN must not use an unverified newly placed tube or crush medications without formulation review.
examTrap: Injecting air and listening over the stomach to confirm tube placement before the first feeding.
oneLinePearl: Feed safely: verified tube, head up, flush, reassess.

title: Acute Liver Failure: Encephalopathy Plus Coagulopathy Is an ICU Emergency
bottomLine: Acute liver failure is rapid severe hepatic dysfunction with coagulopathy and encephalopathy in a patient without established cirrhosis. Monitor airway/mental status, glucose, hemodynamics, bleeding, renal function and cerebral edema risk; give cause-specific therapy such as N-acetylcysteine when ordered and transfer early to a transplant-capable center when indicated.
recognize: Jaundice, nausea, RUQ discomfort followed by confusion/encephalopathy
Hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, renal failure and cerebral edema can develop
Acetaminophen toxicity is a major U.S. cause; drug/herbal/viral/ischemic/autoimmune causes also occur
assess: Serial mental status, pupils, airway, glucose, BP/perfusion, urine output
Medication/toxin history including exact acetaminophen products/doses/time
Trend INR, AST/ALT, bilirubin, glucose, lactate, creatinine/electrolytes as ordered
actions: Emergency hepatology/transplant-center escalation
Airway protection for worsening encephalopathy
Frequent glucose monitoring/treatment
Administer N-acetylcysteine or cause-specific therapy as ordered
diagnostics: Acetaminophen level/timing, viral/autoimmune/toxin studies and imaging identify cause
Very high aminotransferases do not by themselves measure remaining liver function; INR, glucose, lactate, mental status and clinical trajectory matter
medicationSafety: N-acetylcysteine is time sensitive in acetaminophen toxicity and may be used in selected non-acetaminophen ALF
Avoid hepatotoxic/sedating medications when possible and verify doses
teaching: Avoid duplicate acetaminophen-containing products and follow labeled/prescribed dosing
Seek urgent help after significant overdose even before symptoms develop
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN roles in acute liver failure depend on high-acuity setting. Key duties are meticulous neuro/glucose/hemodynamic monitoring and rapid escalation; transplant/antidote strategy is specialist directed.
examTrap: Waiting for jaundice to become severe before treating a known toxic acetaminophen ingestion.
oneLinePearl: Acute liver failure threatens brain, glucose, clotting and kidneys—move early.
